newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Dec CPI advances 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Dec CPI advances 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported December consumer prices rose 0.3 percent, the same increase as the prior month. Minus food and energy, the "core" rate rose 0.1 percent. Experts had expected consumer prices to rise by 0.3.
PHILIP BRAVERMAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DKB SECURITIES INC:
"Actually, it's very favorable that the core is 0.1. The key question that plagues the bond market is whether the rise in energy ... indicates that it's going to filter through to general inflation."
Braverman was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.
ANTHONY CHAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANC ONE INVESTMENT

ADVISORS: "Consumer prices basically followed similar behavior of (producer prices) last month; it was a very good number. So far, it tells us that although there are a lot of growing labor cost pressures, the economy is quite fortunate not to have that show up in higher prices.
"Apparel is an example. Although there had been more purchases of apparel in recent months, it's comforting to see that the apparel component did not show a pick-up in prices."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO
INTERNATIONAL INC: "December is usually not the time for prices to show a large uptick. You usually tend to get price increases early in the year rather than late in the year.

"I did not expect a real problem in the energy (Consumer Price Index) component. It had a good headline, which will probably give the (Treasury) market a temporary lift. But I think ultimately what it comes down to is the strength of the economy."
JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES
CORP: "Pretty tame. A good increase in energy that just doesn't move into the broad constellation of prices, so good news there.

"The (Treasury) market reaction, which has been mostly positive so far, is, I think, a reflection that people were short going into it and more afraid of the CPI than the retail sales number," Liro added.
RAYMOND WORSECK, CHIEF ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS INC:

"The (Treasury) market is paying attention to the fact that the core rate on the CPI is lower than expected. From a (Federal Reserve) policy standpoint, the market is more worried about inflation than a strong economy. If we can have a strong economy without a pick-up in inflation, the Fed's not going to do anything at the February meeting.
"In that sense, if you weigh the morning's two reports, the CPI would have a more positive implication for the market than the retail sales would have a negative one."
December retail sales were also released this morning.
MICHAEL NIEMIRA, ECONOMIST, BANK OF TOKYO-MITSUBISHI LTD:
"It actually was more similar to the feel of the (producer price) report given the pop in energy, yet the core remained well contained, so on that front it was probably good news.

"We've seen higher energy prices now for a number of months and it's not something you can just shrug off and say it's part of the core, however. The fact that energy prices have shot up so much means that discretionary purposes are being limited and that ultimately could slow consumption in the first quarter," he added.
RICHARD BERNER, EXECUTIVE VICE PRESIDENT AND CHIEF
ECONOMIST, MELLON BANK CORP: "(The CPI report) reinforces the perception we're looking at a low-inflation environment. The real issue is what the risks are going forward.
"The number this month is in broad-based terms exceptionally good. Obviously, the energy component was the main factor boosting it.
"Going forward here as the economy heats up, as I think it is doing, inflation risk is going to become one-sided. Any inflation increase will be very gradual and slow in coming."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
